title: The whole household
hookLine: a household that prays, eats and laughs together
tomorrow: the morning after, Amira's prayer feels like nothing. keep going?

cards: A dining table pulled out to its last leaf, folding chairs from the garage, and one more chair than anyone asked for. The doorbell rings in the middle of dinner.
Someone nobody quite expected is on the step, holding a box of sweets. Now what? You pull out the chair, you pass the plate, and somebody says bismillah.
So, one question for today: what turns a house into a household?

teach.b: The tradition's answer is surprisingly ordinary: you eat together, you pray together, you laugh together.
Some men once told the Prophet ﷺ: we eat, but we're never satisfied. Perhaps you eat separately, he said. Eat together and mention God's name over your food, and it will be blessed for you.
That's in Sunan Abu Dawud. In Sahih al-Bukhari he tells a boy in his care, 'Umar ibn Abi Salamah: say bismillah, eat with your right hand, and eat from what's in front of you.
Then the laughing. 'A'isha said she raced the Prophet on a journey and won. Later, after she'd put on weight, they raced again and he won, and he said: this one's for that one. Now a neighbor.
In the Bible's book of Acts, the first Christians are described in the King James words as "breaking bread from house to house, did eat their meat with gladness and singleness of heart."
Gladness at a shared table, blessing in eating together: that hope is shared. And one honest difference.
In some Christian homes, one person says grace for the whole table. In the hadith, even a small boy is told to say God's name himself.
One to tell a friend tonight: the Prophet lost a footrace to his wife, won the rematch, and joked about it.

how: Muslim families say bismillah before eating and alhamdulillah after, and eat from shared dishes; the hadith encourages eating together rather than apart.

o: everyone at home eating, praying, laughing together
the oldest relative who runs the whole family
a house where several generations share bills

games.q: who's who at the table — tap the pairs.

s: eating apart and eating together bring the same blessing
the men who ate separately weren't satisfied; eat together, the Prophet said.
the Prophet raced 'A'isha and lost, then won the rematch
the book of Acts describes early Christians eating together with gladness
breaking bread from house to house.

games.q: your family eats in shifts: dad at the counter, your sister in her room, you on the couch with your phone. what does the Abu Dawud hadith suggest?
o: nothing; what matters is that everyone eats something.
eat together and say God's name; that's where the blessing is.
keep eating apart, as long as each person says bismillah.
games.why: the men who ate separately weren't satisfied. eat together and mention God's name, the Prophet said, and it will be blessed.

practice: Look at the table you eat at most, or picture it if you're away: the chairs, the marks on the wood, who usually sits where. Let your eyes rest on an empty seat, if there is one, and on the person who belongs there, or could.
Stay with that seat for the rest of the time.

wordCard.voice: The whole household: everyone under one roof eating, praying and laughing together, with God's name said at the table.

orig.note: Arabic: in the name of God; said before eating.

carryVoice: The last line of ten: one household, one table, a bismillah from every chair. Family and friendship, complete.

sources.ref: Sunan Abu Dawud 3764 (we eat and are not satisfied; perhaps you eat separately; eat together and mention God's name, and it will be blessed for you)
